articles.title: Generate Tenant Report Files with Presigned Download URLs and Explicit Retention
articles.excerpt: TL;DR: to generate a presigned URL for a file download in S3-compatible Node.js storage, authorize the customer first, then sign a short-lived GET request for the exact object key. Return it to the cl…
articles.body: TL;DR: to generate a presigned URL for a file download in S3-compatible Node.js storage, authorize the customer first, then sign a short-lived GET request for the exact object key. Return it to the client and treat deletion as a separate retention workflow. The URL is a capability, not an authorization system. For a B2B SaaS export, the decision boundary is simple: a presigned link fits a customer download that can go directly to object storage, while tenant ownership, retention, and deletion stay in the database and workers. A 60-second link can reduce load on the application server. It cannot decide if a report should still exist. The signature is not the policy. That is the catch.

articles.body: An AI agent is only as reliable as the actions it performs. While large language models have become increasingly capable of reasoning and generating responses, production-grade agentic systems require something more: measurable tool execution reliability. Selecting an incorrect API, generating invalid arguments, or misinterpreting an execution result can cause significant problems in real-world applications. This article explores research-backed approaches to evaluating AI agents. 1. Why Traditional LLM Evaluation Is Not Enough Traditional LLM evaluation primarily focuses on response accuracy, relevance, coherence, and factual correctness.

articles.title: Hackers were inside the Air Force's cloud. An upgrade found them, not security.
articles.excerpt: Hackers got into Cloud One, the US Air Force's main cloud platform. Reuters broke it on Friday, and a US official confirmed it to NBC. The Air Force itself won't comment. This isn't some side system.…
articles.body: Hackers got into Cloud One, the US Air Force's main cloud platform. Reuters broke it on Friday, and a US official confirmed it to NBC. The Air Force itself won't comment. This isn't some side system. Cloud One is the "one-stop shop" they built in 2017. It runs air defense radar feeds for North America, munitions tracking across 200+ bases, and personnel and logistics data. Here's the part I can't stop thinking about. It wasn't a security alert that caught it. It turned up while people were doing upgrade work on the system. Read that again. The military's flagship cloud, and the thing that found the intruders was a routine upgrade. I don't think that's an Air Force problem. I think that's how most breaches actually get found.

articles.title: Why putting a secret in a system prompt never works
articles.excerpt: A shop chatbot has a rule in its system prompt: never reveal the discount code. The code is right there in the same prompt. How long does it stay secret once a user starts asking? Usually not long, an…
articles.body: A shop chatbot has a rule in its system prompt: never reveal the discount code. The code is right there in the same prompt. How long does it stay secret once a user starts asking? Usually not long, and the reason is structural. One stream of text A language model gets a single sequence of tokens. Your system prompt is the start of it. The user's message comes after. There is no separate, protected channel for instructions, so the rule "never reveal the code" is competing with whatever the user typed next. Vendors train models to prefer the system prompt, which raises the effort needed. It does not remove the problem. How a test usually goes Picture a tester working through a retail bot that holds a promo code. Ask directly. The bot refuses. Ask for the instructions.

articles.body: Testopslag fra ACX Værktøj. Vi afprøver planlagt udgivelse med en lille PNG. Målet er at undersøge, hvad en læser faktisk kan hente, når en virksomhed udgiver en artikel med et billede. Vi begynder med originalen. Billedet er 384 × 128 pixel og fylder 9.108 byte. Inden udgivelsen beregner vi filens SHA-256 og gemmer resultatet sammen med målene. Så har vi noget konkret at sammenligne med. Når artiklen er ude, henter vi først den offentlige artikel uden cookies og følger billedets adresse fra artikelteksten. Vi tjekker både filtypen og dimensionerne. En server kan godt svare med 200 og alligevel vise en fejlside. Vi beregner også en SHA-256 for de hentede byte. Hvis tallene er ens, er filerne byte for byte identiske.

articles.title: How moon dust and recycled cardboard could help NASA build its lunar base
articles.excerpt: The high cost of building on the moon has led to wide-ranging research on how to make use of the moon's most plentiful resource: the dusty regolith that covers its surface.
articles.body: The high cost of building on the moon has led to wide-ranging research on how to make use of the moon's most plentiful resource: the dusty regolith that covers its surface. Right now, lunar shipping runs about $544,000 per pound ($1.2 million per kilogram), so anything that astronauts can make on the moon using existing materials could help a lot. Scientists have already proposed using regolith for building 3D-printed bricks , solar arrays , and even as soil to grow potatoes . Now, a team of researchers from Purdue University in Indiana have developed an aerogel made from simulated regolith for insulating lunar habitats. New aerogels created by Purdue University researchers, made of cellulose and lunar regolith simulant, could pave the way for insulating materials made on the moon.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 28, 1967: Astronomers Jocelyn Bell and Antony Hewish disover the 1st pulsar with Little Green Men 1 signal
articles.excerpt: On November 28, 1967, astronomers found the first pulsar and they called the signal Little Green Men 1. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On November 28, 1967, astronomers found the first pulsar. A pulsar is a super-dense star that rotates super fast. As the pulsar spins, it emits two beams of light in opposite directions. When astronomers look at a pulsar, it looks like a star that's flickering on and off at a steady, constant pace. The first pulsar was observed by Jocelyn Bell Burnell and Antony Hewish. They were looking at the constellation Vulpecula when they saw a star flickering with regular pulses separated by 1.33 seconds. At first they had no idea what it was, so they jokingly nicknamed the signal Little Green Men 1. After more pulsars were discovered, they were able to rule out aliens. This chart tracked the signal of the first pulsar ever discoverered on Nov. 28, 1967.
